newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urges governors not to divert welfare savings.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges governors not to divert welfare savings.

text.p: President Bill Clinton told the nation's 50 state governors on Monday it would be a "big mistake" to divert savings from welfare reform to other programmes, and urged them to use the money to provide jobs, transportation and child care for the poor.

"I know there are big debates in some state capitols about how to use extra money caused by the fact...that the (welfare) case load is much lower in your states," Clinton said. "But I think if we were to divert these savings to other things, it would be a big mistake."

The president said such a move would "come home to haunt the states" the next time there was an economic downturn because the number of people on public assistance, now at the lowest level since 1970, would skyrocket.

"Even in an economic downturn, if people lose their jobs, if they have work experience now, then when they become unemployed...they will be far, far more likely to be unemployed for a shorter period of time," he said.

Clinton's speech at a meeting of the National Governor's Association (NGA) came as the White House and Congressional Republicans worked toward agreement on final details of legislation that will cut taxes and balance the budget by 2002.

A five-term governor of Arkansas who once led the NGA, Clinton said he found it "terribly nostalgic" to meet his former colleagues. The meeting was relatively brief, however. After his speech, Clinton played a round of golf with some of the governors and basketball superstar Michael Jordan.

On the last leg of a three-day trip through the U.S. West that mixed business and recreation, Clinton said he was optimistic about the budget talks in Washington, describing them as in the "final stage."
"This is an historic opportunity. It would be the achievement of a generation...and I believe we're on the verge of achieving it," Clinton told the governors.

He said he expected the package to provide $3 billion over the next five years to help states create "work opportunities" for people on public assistance, who under the new welfare reform law must find jobs after two years on the welfare rolls. The law also places a five-year lifetime limit on welfare benefits.
Clinton said child care, transportation and tough enforcement of child support were also "critical steps" in moving people from welfare to work.

Noting that only six percent of the welfare recipients owned their own vehicles, Clinton asked the governors to press Congress to approve his proposal to spend $600 million to enable states and communities to help those on welfare get to and from work.
